title: Library Management System
summary: A gentle first LLD case study: modeling a catalog, its physical copies, members, holds, and borrowing rules — where Book vs BookItem is the whole lesson.

slides.markdown:
A library management system models a **catalog**, its **physical copies**, **members**, and the rules for borrowing them. It's the standard first LLD case study because it looks simple but hides a real subtlety: a book *title* and a physical *copy* of that title are different things, and conflating them is the first mistake most candidates make.

Think of the catalog like a card index and the copies like the actual books on the shelf — many people can browse the same title, but only as many people as there are copies can hold one at a time.

**In scope:** a searchable catalog of titles, tracking each physical copy independently, member registration, checkout and return, a hold/reservation queue for titles that are fully checked out, and per-member-type fines.

**Out of scope:** a recommendation engine, self-checkout kiosk hardware, and inter-library loans — cutting these up front stops the design from sprawling into a much bigger system than what's being asked.

Stating non-goals out loud is itself a signal in an interview: it shows you can bound a problem instead of designing everything you can think of.

**Book** is the catalog entry — title, author, ISBN — one row no matter how many copies exist. **BookItem** is one physical copy — it has a barcode, a condition, and a status (`AVAILABLE`, `ON_HOLD`, `CHECKED_OUT`, `LOST`). A library might have one `Book` row for *Clean Code* but three `BookItem` rows, one per physical copy on the shelf.

`Member`, `Loan`, and `Reservation` round out the model: a `Loan` links one `Member` to one `BookItem` for a date range, and a `Reservation` queues a `Member` against a `Book` title, not a specific copy — you reserve *a copy of this title*, not copy #47 specifically.

Conflating `Book` and `BookItem` is the most common mistake here: if availability lives on the title instead of per copy, you can't tell which physical book someone actually holds, or how many are left.

![Class diagram: Book linked one-to-many to BookItem, with Member, Loan, and Reservation as related entities](assets/book-bookitem-model.svg)

The key relationship is `Book` one-to-many `BookItem`: one catalog row, many physical copies, each tracked independently. `Loan` binds a `Member` to a specific `BookItem`; `Reservation` binds a `Member` to a `Book` title, since you reserve a title before any specific copy is free.

Fines and hold expiry hang off `Loan` and `Reservation` rather than bloating `Member` or `BookItem` with fields that only apply sometimes.

assets.alt: Class diagram: Book linked one-to-many to BookItem, with Member, Loan, and Reservation as related entities

slides.sectionTitle: Holds as their own entity, not a flag
slides.markdown:
A tempting shortcut is a boolean `isReserved` on `BookItem`. It breaks almost immediately: a hold needs to know *who* requested it, *where* they are in the queue if several members want the same sold-out title, and *when* their claim expires once a copy frees up.

Model it as a `Reservation` entity instead: `member`, `book`, `queuePosition`, `status` (`WAITING`, `READY`, `EXPIRED`, `FULFILLED`), and `expiresAt`. Reservations for one title form a FIFO queue ordered by creation time.

This is the same lesson as `Loan` vs a raw `checkedOutBy` field on `BookItem` — anything with its own identity, timeline, or ordering deserves its own class, not a field bolted onto something else.

![State machine: BookItem moving between AVAILABLE, CHECKED_OUT, ON_HOLD, and a dead-end LOST_OR_DAMAGED branch](assets/bookitem-lifecycle.svg)

A copy starts `AVAILABLE`. Checkout moves it to `CHECKED_OUT`. On return it normally goes straight back to `AVAILABLE` — unless the title has a waiting reservation, in which case it becomes `ON_HOLD` for the next member in line instead.

The `LOST_OR_DAMAGED` branch off `CHECKED_OUT` is a dead end for that physical copy: it never returns to `AVAILABLE` and instead triggers a separate replacement workflow.

assets.alt: State machine: BookItem moving between AVAILABLE, CHECKED_OUT, ON_HOLD, and a dead-end LOST_OR_DAMAGED branch

slides.sectionTitle: Strategy for fine policy, not Observer for holds
slides.markdown:
Two design-pattern decisions show up in the same topic, and picking the wrong one in each direction is a common interview stumble.

| Decision | Pattern used | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Fine/loan rules per member type (student, faculty, guest) | **Strategy** | Each member type's rate and loan period is genuinely different behavior, swapped at runtime per member |
| Notifying the next holder when a copy frees up | **Deliberately no Observer** | A scheduled job scanning hold queues every few minutes is simpler, and the notification isn't latency-sensitive |

**How to decide:** reach for a pattern when it removes a real `if/else` chain that will keep growing (fine policy will keep adding member types); skip one when a dumber mechanism — polling, a cron job — already meets the actual requirement without added machinery.

slides.sectionTitle: The hard part: FIFO holds get first refusal
slides.markdown:
When the last checked-out copy of a popular title comes back, it can't just flip to `AVAILABLE` — if there's a hold queue, the front of that queue gets **first refusal**: the system notifies them and starts an expiry timer (say, 48 hours) before offering the copy to anyone else, including a plain walk-in checkout.

This is the piece candidates most often skip, because a naive `returnItem()` only knows about the copy, not about demand for the title. The fix is for return to check the title's reservation queue *before* deciding the item's new status.

Miss this and two things go wrong: a member who's been waiting weeks loses their spot to someone who happened to walk in first, and the queue never actually drains.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: BookItem.returnItem() checks the hold queue
Compare: one Book class vs Book + BookItem
slides.markdown:
| | Single `Book` class | `Book` + `BookItem` |
|---|---|---|
| Catalog fields (title, author, ISBN) | Duplicated per physical copy | Stored once, shared by all copies |
| Per-copy state (condition, barcode, current holder) | Bolted onto the same row, awkward with multiple copies | Naturally lives on `BookItem` |
| "How many copies are left?" | Requires a separate counter kept in sync by hand | A `COUNT` over `BookItem` rows in `AVAILABLE` status |
| Damaging one copy | Ambiguous which "copy" you even mean | Marks exactly one `BookItem` as `LOST`, others unaffected |

**How to decide:** the moment a title can exist as more than one physical unit with independent state, split catalog data from inventory data — a single class only holds up for a one-copy-per-title toy version.

slides.sectionTitle: Concurrency: two members, one last copy
slides.markdown:
Two members both hit "checkout" on the last available copy of a popular title within milliseconds of each other. If checkout does a read-then-write — check `status == AVAILABLE`, then set `CHECKED_OUT` — both requests can read `AVAILABLE` before either write lands, and both walk away thinking they have the book.

The fix is the same **atomic reserve-then-confirm pattern** used for the last parking spot or the last movie seat: the status flip must be a single conditional update (`UPDATE book_item SET status='CHECKED_OUT' WHERE id=? AND status='AVAILABLE'`) or an equivalent compare-and-swap, and only the request whose update actually affected a row wins. A post-hoc "check again after checkout" re-check is too late — the race already happened.

The general rule: never let two threads separately read a piece of shared state, decide based on the stale read, and then write — collapse read-decide-write into one atomic operation.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: fine logic living inside Member
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Fines are a member's business, so `Member.calculateFine()` should just have an if/else for student vs faculty vs guest rates."

**Why it's wrong:** every new member type or policy change — a grace period for faculty, a cap for students — means editing `Member` again, and `Member` accumulates unrelated responsibilities (identity, loans, *and* every fine rule that has ever existed). This is exactly the single-responsibility violation that shows up across LLD problems: a class that changes for more than one reason.

**Correct model:** extract a `FinePolicy` interface with one method, `calculateFine(loan)`, and give each member type a policy object it delegates to. Adding a new member type or rate becomes a new class, not an edit to `Member`.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: skipping the hold queue on return
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Returning a book just means marking the `BookItem` available again."

**Why it's wrong:** it silently strands every member who placed a hold on that title. The book becomes free, but instead of reaching the first person in the FIFO queue, it's grabbed by whoever happens to check availability next — the interviewer will absolutely ask "what happens to the people who reserved it?" and this design has no answer.

**Correct model:** `returnItem()` must consult `Book.nextWaitingReservation()` before deciding the new status — if a queue exists, the item goes to `ON_HOLD` for that member with an expiry, and only falls through to plain `AVAILABLE` when the queue is empty.
